Wake Up Dead Man brings a fresh burst of energy into the mystery genre, blending sharp storytelling with a confident visual style that feels both modern and timeless. From the opening moments, the film establishes a tone that's playful yet purposeful, inviting the audience not just to watch, but to participate in the mystery.The direction is stylish without being distracting-every shot feels deliberate, often hiding meaning in small details that reward careful viewers. Dialogue is one of the film's biggest strengths: witty, layered, and delivered with just the right mix of charm and tension. The cast clearly understands the rhythm of this world, and their performances strike a balance between grounded emotion and a slightly heightened, almost theatrical energy that suits the genre well.What truly elevates the film is its confidence. It doesn't rush to impress with cheap twists; instead, it builds intrigue step by step, trusting the audience to keep up. There's a subtle escalation throughout that keeps you engaged, guessing, and occasionally second-guessing every character on screen.A clever, confidently crafted mystery film that respects its audience and delivers tension, humor, and style in equal measure-without spoiling the pleasure of discovery.

Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery is a fine third iteration of the classic whodunnit mystery within the Knives Out franchise.To review this film, you have to either write a lengthy passage reflecting on all the themes the film shines light on, or make it short and simple. I'll go simple on this one.The script is just an imprint of Rian Johnson's thoughts and style. And since supposedly nobody was keeping Rian at bay, the first probably 30 minutes of the film felt unhinged when it comes to humor and satire. The film almost turned into a meta-comedy in the second act, but still managed to get back to the mystery it was intended to untangle.The story was a classic Rian Johnson's one with excessive childish humor, lots of callbacks and nods to other franchises, constant attempt at subverting the viewer's expectations.At the same time, it had lots of interesting political, personal and religious themes discussed, like (obviously) faith, religion, moral values and personal choices, greed, manipulation, power and politics, media and social interactions. While Rian surely wanted to have fresh characters and not basic stereotypes, some of them were still loosely connected to the story if at all, and felt more like tokens with traits attached rather than characters. The plot was well-constructed, but few scenes still felt like the plot was giving itself a push forward after stumbling and loosing it's focus.Some might say that the film bashes on religion (especially in the first 30 minutes), but didn't find the film offensive in this way. The ending perfectly shows the respect given to genuine faith and canonical moral values.The cast managed to deliver great performances with no exceptions, probably due to good direction, although in my opinion Andrew Scott was just underused, really needed more of him in this film.Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery is a prefect blend of political, religious and other personal themes, wrapped into classic Johnson's excessive whodunnit buffoonery. A solid 8/10, thank you, Rian Johnson.

Knives Out was such a gem of a film, Glass Onion felt too convoluted, this one goes even further down that path. Supporting cast were great but didn't have much chance to flex their muscle. Wake Up Dead Man has a strong final act, but it doesn't come close to justifying the mess that precedes it.When the film finally slows down, tightens its focus, and lets its themes breathe, it works. The last act brings real tension, stronger performances, and a sense of purpose that's been missing for most of the runtime. Unfortunately, it takes far too long to get there.The first two thirds are bloated with unnecessary characters who are introduced rapidly and then contribute almost nothing. This never needed to be an ensemble mystery, yet it insists on being one, seemingly more interested in parading recognisable faces than telling a coherent story. Several characters feel completely redundant, and some (Mila Kunis' police chief) strain credibility to the point of distraction.Even Benoit Blanc's introduction is mishandled. After a major death, the case is almost immediately labelled "impossible to solve," without any real buildup or failed investigation. We're told the mystery is unsolvable before we've had any chance to engage with it. Blanc suddenly appears out of thin air because the script demands it, not because the story naturally pulls him in, which undercuts tension from the outset.Character motivation is another weak spot. Monsignor Jefferson Wicks is portrayed as openly hostile early on, yet this behaviour makes little sense given what we later learn. His meanness feels less like intentional characterisation and more like a shortcut to create false suspicion, especially since key information only comes to light much later.The pacing only adds to the problem. Scenes arrive quickly, but the story itself barely moves, leaving the film feeling both rushed and oddly stagnant.By the end, Wake Up Dead Man proves it could have been a sharp, character driven mystery. Instead, it's an overstuffed and uneven film that mistakes excess for depth. The final act earns it a very generous 5/10, but everything before it drags that score down.

Let me preface this review by saying that I consider myself a moderate, because, sadly, a murder mystery by Rian Johnson needs to be all about politics.Watching this movie made me remember that comic strip where a man is yelling: "Racist! Bigot! Another racist!" only to be revealed that he is in psychotherapy and looking at Rorschach inkblots. Similarly to that, Rian Johnson is obsessed by some imaginary evil right wing misogynists, racists and bigots, so he used this movie to try to make fun of them in such a clumsy and intense way that you have to be worried about his mental wellbeing. Such is the intensity of Rian's obsession, that you want to quote that meme and ask him "are those racists in the room with us now?" And the lame attempt at "meta" humor, when one of the characters says how the story will end up on Netflix and all of them will be played by some lame versions of themselves is just a pathetic attempt to immunize the movie from the criticism it thoroughly deserves.You could actually argue that there are two movies in here. One is Rian's paranoid delusional mania about the right wingers that he feels so threatened by, and the other is a murder mystery. The mystery is not terrible, but mediocre, the characters are uninteresting, the run time is twice what it should be, and the revelation is convoluted and by the time it comes, you don't care about it any more. Rian's mania, on the other hand, is just sad. In his world of boogeymen right wingers and evil religion, the only good priests are the ones who speak like gangster rappers, and it is OK to steal inheritance from people if they are republicans. Still, his inability to show his personal views without beating the viewers over the head with them is well known. Cue the Glass Onion, which was even worse than this movie.Acting by Josh Brolin and Glenn Close is great, while Craig is all over the place with his whatever accent coming and going at random intervals, and the actor who plays the young priest just seems lost.If you agree with Rian's political views, I guess that you will like this movie. If, on the other hand, you like a good murder mystery, and/or actually rely on reason and facts when thinking about politics, you should probably skip it.

It's well acted, well paced, and it captures the enormity of the trials. But as I watched I couldn't help feeling like it only brushed the surface of something far more complex, which is the psychology of the men being judged.The film touches on it here and there with glimpses of pride, denial, rationalization, but never quite lets us sit in their mindset long enough to understand how such thinking takes root. I don't mean sympathy, but understanding.Most films about this era stay safely on the side of "righteousness". A movie that truly follows the "bad" side, that dares to dissect the Nazi perspective without flinching could make one of the most unsettling and important films ever made. Nuremberg is strong, but it leaves that untold story still waiting for someone brave enough to tell it.Maybe the reason the psychiatrist ends up committing 13 years later is because he was having a moral debate with himself over the trials and the "good" and "bad".

I had so many expectations for this movie, but unfortunately it couldn't fulfill them all. I can say that this film has actually distorted history in some places and has not shown the events as they were. If you have watched the film carefully and are someone who has read history, or even if you have not read history but have a curious mind, you will come across these flaws with a simple investigation. First of all, I really admire Russell Crowe's performance in this film. One of the most fundamental things that was not shown in this film was Hermann Göring's weight loss. In reality, Göring had become so thin that he looked small in his clothes, and this historical fact was not shown at all in the film. Another fundamental and important fact was that Hermann Göring never used the words "Long Live Hitler" in court, and none of the surviving documents from the Nuremberg Trials show this, while in the film we see her uttering such a statement in front of everyone in court. Another issue that could have been shown in the film but wasn't was Hermann Göring's mockery of the trial, which actually happened. In court, Göring sometimes behaved as if he were the judge and actually sometimes beat the prosecutor, and this was not shown in the film. One of the other most important things that was not shown in the film but happened in reality was Göring giving the military salute at the first trial. (A normal military salute with a right hand next to the temple, not the Nazi military salute.) There are many such facts, none of which were shown in the film, and the main focus was more on the psychologist than on Göring himself and the things he did in court. We immediately see that his court session is shown very little in the film and only occurs in two parts. Well, for a film called Nuremberg and reminiscent of the Nuremberg Trials, this was a very wrong and weak act. It could have been much better and stronger, but unfortunately it didn't meet all my expectations, but overall it was an entertaining film and Hermann Göring was played beautifully by the actor.

7.7/10 (Recommend)First reaction is that this movie deserves to be commended on more than saying the acting was good, the story was heavy, and the pacing was decent. All three of these things ring true, but it was also more than that. It was thought provoking in its humanity, morality, and legality.So here is my checklist of this film:The acting was good, but I don't think any of it was award winning. The variety of actors chosen for each role made everything feel genuine for the era. Most impressive was Russell Crowe actually speaking German. I assumed it would be him speaking English the entire time, but with a German accent. Beyond the acting feeling authentic the sets felt real too. There wasn't just a ton of close-up shots trying to convince you that you were in war torn Germany. They gave you brief avenues to truly see.The story was heavy. You know why they're in Nuremberg, and you know the atrocities that took place. But you know when you don't hear a single crunching of popcorn or rustling of snacks, and there's a collective holding of breath, then you know the director has reeled you in. (Humanity) Emotionally it was more pain and hurt seeing the atrocities and not just tear jerking.The pacing was good. Despite its 2.5 hour runtime, the pacing was enjoyable. There's very few moments of down time. I would recommend not going to see the film if you've either been sitting all day, or are tired, or both. I was restless throughout because of both of those things.The legality and morality of Nuremberg was not something I ever really considered before. These trials were unprecedented and so the cases had to be built from the ground up. It only shows a partiality of this, but it goes just deep enough to give you a sense.Overall, this is a movie I'd recommend seeing in theatres. The sound quality is spectacular and the visuals are great on the big screen. This isn't an award winning film by any stretch of the imagination, but it does its job well enough to say "these were some of the first men to be tried in Nuremberg. We try to humanize them, but in the end they are evil." It might be long for some, but for others it's good entertainment and possibly the beginning of a knowledge quest.That's it for now. Thanks for taking time to read my review. Happy watching and enjoy the show!

Despite its impressive cast, "Nuremberg" never rises above the level of a standard blockbuster. Russell Crowe delivers a charismatic performance as Hermann Göring, capturing both his charm and menace. Rami Malek, as the American psychologist, is equally convincing, if sometimes deliberately irritating. But strong acting alone can't save the film from its shallow storytelling and predictable structure. The final act slips into a clichéd hero narrative, where the psychologist suddenly redeems himself in a scene that feels more tiresome than triumphant. Eventually, the film's attempt at a pointe isn't misguided, but it feels forced.

This film was incredibly good. The soundtrack was spectacular, in the cinema you could just FEEL the historic weight of the events the film centers around. The pacing was also perfect, for a historic drama, its 140 minutes felt incredibly short. The cast and the acting was great as well. But most importantly, the deeper meaning and the messages of the film are just so important, and were delivered spectacularly. You just walk out with a pit in your stomach.I still had some minor problems with the film, for example that it has some of the classic Hollywood US-centrism. I appreciate that the film was based mainly on a book, focusing on the relationship between the american psychiatrist and Göring, but I would have loved some more focus on other important figures. We didn't hear one single word from a russian or french judge or prosecutor for example. Some moments also felt a bit too unrealistic or theatrical for me, Jacksons meeting with the pope comes to mind, or the role and treatment of the psychiatrist in some parts. Also, it would have been great if Görings actor could have been german, but Russell Crowe makes up for it with an incredible performance, so I'll let that one go.All in all the positives far outweigh the negatives for me though. A highly important, thought-provoking and entertaining film.

The positive. It's very well acted, perfectly paced, has good cinematography. Overall it's a compelling peice of cinema. It does maintain tension.However, it's not without substantive flaws. The dialogue is written to be too modern - slightly too informal for the period, even for informal speech, lacking plausible idiom and missing some period wording. What starts as potentially an interesting character study on Göring, as well as historically significant slice of time, as the run time moves on, collapses into familiar moral shorthand surrounding the Holocaust, and in doing so looses it's most interesting tension.And that is understandable of course, but it's very explored territory, and doesn't offer any fresh understanding of the Nazi's, or the Allies. Indeed it romanticizes the egalitarianism of the Allies, in a way that doesn't accurately reflect the West, or the United States, in 1945. It, like so many others, mythologizes historical events with a modern culture lens, and plays it safe.In summary, one might hope for more literary style realism at the start of this film, but it feels trapped by the same post-ww2 modern framework. It's still a compelling film, but short of it's potential.

Of course this is an important topic and it's a story that needs to be told. If nothing else to help us better understand the motivations that can lead people to such evil.A great cast has been assembled and there is a great movie to be made. But this isn't it. It's far from terrible but I came away thinking it was a bit meh as a piece of art. Take nothing away from the actors who did a fine job, especially the leads.Maybe in the age of the streamers where stories are told in great depth over many episodes and seasons, it becomes tougher to present significant work in a 2hr frame.For me it felt superficial, in the sense that there were countless opportunities to dig deeper into characters and relationships but, in the urge to cover ground, it felt like we skimmed the surface only.It felt pedestrian. Obviously in fact-based stories the base facts are known so there can be little tension or jeopardy associated with storyline. But I felt we could have gone way deeper on the people, their personalities and their relationships. I saw this film at the AFI Film Fest in Hollywood. Also interesting was the part that Sgt. Howie Triest (Leo Woodhall) played during the trial - I had not heard of his story before, and I have read and studied a lot about WWII. Russell Crowe is brilliant as Goering and Malek is very good but not perfect. Now for some of the issues I have the film. The portrayal of Goering on the witness stand was very good, but it was not accurate - the movie implies that it was all in one day and it was not. Also, I did not like Slattery's over the top performance as the warden of the prison. Michael Shannon's performance as Justice Jackson was adequate but not compelling or accurate. There are some other minor inaccuracies that cause me to delete a couple of points from an otherwise excellent film, but I definitely recommend it for fans of fine drama.

Hermann Göring (Russell Crowe), Hitler's right-hand man, is imprisoned after the fall of Nazi Germany alongside other high-ranking leaders. Psychiatrist Douglas Kelley (Rami Malek) is tasked with assessing Göring's mental state and determining his role within the Nazi hierarchy. Meanwhile, Justice Robert H. Jackson (Michael Shannon) prepares for the prosecution. As Douglas becomes increasingly fascinated, even charmed, by Göring's intellect and manipulation, he begins to doubt whether Jackson can truly outmatch him in the courtroom.Rami Malek, Michael Shannon, Richard E. Grant, and Colin Firth deliver committed performances. Malek has a few standout emotional moments that genuinely elevate the script. Shannon is characteristically sharp, though his presence is frustratingly limited. Richard E. Grant's Sir David Maxwell-Fyfe dominates the last scene, unintentionally overshadowing Shannon simply because his character is written with more bite.As for Russell Crowe: he doesn't quite disappear into Göring. He's still Russell Crowe, the face of Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind, the familiar physical presence. The added weight may mirror Göring's later years, but it doesn't add psychological heft to his performance. Someone like Kevin Spacey chilling, calm, reptilian might have captured the unnerving charisma of Göring with more authenticity. Crowe feels more like a well-known actor performing a war criminal than inhabiting one.The film is long and feels long. Several scenes, especially the extended philosophical conversations between Douglas and Howie, play like filler: moments that pad the runtime rather than deepen the narrative.The story often circles around its ideas instead of advancing them, resulting in a movie that's about war crimes, guilt, accountability, and manipulation... yet somehow lacks urgency.There are sharp moments. When Rami Malek hits emotional gear, you feel it. When Grant enters the courtroom, the dialogue finally snaps to life. But these highlights are too sparse to rescue the entire film. And with such a powerful cast, expectations were naturally high maybe too high for the uneven script to sustain.Nuremberg brings together a heavyweight cast to dramatize the psychological chess match behind the post-WWII trials, but despite the pedigree, the film never reaches the emotional or historical gravity it aims for.Nuremberg is respectable, watchable, and occasionally gripping, but never fully compelling. With this cast, the movie should have hit harder. Instead, it lands somewhere in the middle: thoughtful, but not profound; well-acted, but not transformative; long, but not deep.

Nuremberg (2025) :
Movie Review -Stanley Kramer made many good films in his career, but Judgment at Nuremberg easily surpasses them all and remains one of my most cherished films of the 1960s. While Hollywood at the time was basking in colorful romantic comedies and anti-war dramas, this black-and-white courtroom tale about the aftermath of Nazi atrocities made all those films look colorless. Reimagining or rediscovering this monumental story six decades later was never going to be easy, nor was it ever possible to match the cinematic legacy of Kramer's masterpiece. Yet, I appreciate that the filmmakers at least tried to explore something new - a psychological perspective rather than a legal one. The 2025 version of Nuremberg unfolds not in the courtroom but inside the mind of a psychiatrist. The film is told largely from the perspective of Dr. Douglas Kelley (Rami Malek), a chief psychiatrist assigned to assess the mental state of Nazi officials before their trials. This shift in focus leaves less room for the kind of gripping courtroom exchanges that defined the 1961 original - a decision that ultimately weakens the film's dramatic punch. However, despite its uneven storytelling, Nuremberg offers a few shocking and powerful moments that deserve acknowledgment.The story begins ahead of the historic trials, as Dr. Kelley arrives at the prison to evaluate whether the Nazi war criminals are fit to stand trial. Among them is Hermann Göring played by Russell Crowe, in one of his most commanding late-career performances. Douglas, sharp and analytical, quickly finds himself drawn into a psychological chess match with Göring, who manipulates conversations with unsettling ease. What starts as a routine evaluation soon turns into a dangerous intellectual duel. The more Douglas studies Göring, the more he realizes that this man, despite being a monster, is incredibly intelligent - perhaps even one step ahead of him. Göring's every word, every smile, and every calculated silence reveal that he has meticulously planned his defense, right from his surrender to the courtroom proceedings. Douglas' challenge, then, is to find a way to outsmart him and ensure that justice prevails - ideally with the death penalty that Göring so richly deserves.As mentioned earlier, this version of Nuremberg focuses more on the psychological warfare between doctor and prisoner than on the moral and legal debates that defined the original. The 1961 film remains one of the greatest courtroom dramas ever made, known for its striking cinematography, powerful dialogues, and moral gravity. In contrast, this new film seems visually flat and emotionally uneven. The courtroom scenes lack tension, the debates feel half-hearted, and the production doesn't even attempt to recreate the haunting grandeur of Kramer's vision.Yet, one sequence stands out above all - the concentration camp footage. The moment those images appear on screen, the audience, much like the characters within the film, is left speechless. The horror, the inhumanity, and the raw documentation of suffering cut through the mediocrity of the rest of the film. That brief sequence alone carries the emotional weight that much of the film fails to sustain. Unfortunately, once that moment passes, the narrative returns to its middling rhythm. The confrontations between Hermann and Douglas, the prosecution's strategies, and the courtroom exchanges all lack the emotional depth and sense of urgency that the subject matter demands.Still, the performances elevate the film considerably. Russell Crowe once again proves that he doesn't need elaborate direction or flashy writing to command attention. His portrayal of Göring is layered, frightening, and yet disturbingly charismatic. The German accent, the smug composure, and the subtle psychological manipulation - all are delivered with Crowe's signature intensity. Meanwhile, Rami Malek delivers a performance that often rivals, and occasionally surpasses, Crowe's. As Dr. Douglas Kelley, he portrays curiosity, moral confusion, and internal conflict with admirable restraint. I have admired Malek since Bohemian Rhapsody, and this role reinforces his range and maturity as an actor. The supporting cast - including Leo Woodall, John Slattery, Colin Hanks, Mark O'Brien, Wrenn Schmidt, Lydia Peckham, Michael Shannon, and Richard E. Grant - contributes solid performances that round out the ensemble.Where the film falters most is in its technical execution. The cinematography is disappointingly ordinary - a serious letdown given the historical depth and emotional potential of the subject. The editing feels inconsistent and doesn't build tension effectively. The art direction, though passable, never immerses the viewer in post-war Germany. Even the background score feels muted, rarely enhancing the mood or atmosphere. The opening shot - a man urinating on a Nazi emblem - hints at a provocative tone, but that audacity vanishes soon after. Director James Vanderbilt keeps the story grounded in realism and authenticity, but his approach lacks cinematic fire. The pacing drags, and the tone remains too subdued for a story of such moral and historical magnitude. What's missing here is the courage to confront the darkness with full force. Kramer's Judgment at Nuremberg didn't just depict history - it made viewers feel its moral anguish. This new Nuremberg merely observes it. It's a psychological study that forgets to engage the heart. The film had the potential to be sharper, more brutal, and more introspective, but it settles for being "watchable" rather than unforgettable. And yet, for all its flaws, Nuremberg isn't a total misfire. It deserves credit for revisiting a crucial chapter of history and for attempting to interpret it through a fresh lens. Some scenes - especially those involving the camp footage and the verbal duels between Malek and Crowe - linger long after the credits roll. They remind us that beneath the film's surface lies the echo of something powerful, something that could have been extraordinary with a stronger vision.In short, Nuremberg is a noble effort that falls short of greatness. It neither dishonors the original nor comes close to matching its brilliance. What it offers instead is a modern, psychologically inclined take on the same story - flawed but fascinating in moments. For history enthusiasts and fans of the actors involved, it's worth a viewing. But for those who have witnessed the timeless impact of the 1961 masterpiece, this new chapter will likely feel like an echo - faint, uneven, and yearning for the gravitas of its predecessor.RATING - 5/10*

Probably the best new movie I have seen in a very long time. Great performances and interesting plotlines. The "cat and mouse" relationship between Malek and Crowe is ever changing and complex. One of the best films I've seen in years, and I've seen many. Great performances across the board! I loved it! I simply couldn't stop watching! This one has awards written all over it. Nuremberg tells an important story, not very well, not in a memorable way, but not in a totally false way. It's a Hollywood blockbuster in style, fudging and over-simplifying the narrative as these blockbusters tends to do, and tending to overdramatise the US involvement. The film-makers here made decisions which cluttered the narrative with side stories (the pope's story was an invention, and the translator's story was a quite unnecessary distraction). The scriptwriters couldn't decide whether this was a prisoner-psychologist story or a prosecutor-defendant-trial story so they skimmed through both narratives rather too briefly. And there were lots of very strangely filmed encounters, a dark nighttime conversation at the Nuremberg rally arena in particular. Russell Crowe was OK, but Rami Malek was poorly cast as the psychologist. And two psychologists in an angry body fight in seemingly empty prison corridor...that would never have happened!

Nuremberg (2025)
This film works as a gripping and well-made courtroom drama that keeps you invested from start to finish. This is a well told story of a little known part of the Nuremberg trials. It's a message-laden historical drama about the 1946 Nuremberg trials. We meet Hermann Göring (Russell Crowe) when he is captured after the war, as well as a few lesser lights like Rudolf Hess (Andreas Pietschmann), Julius Streicher (Dieter Riesle), and Robert Ley (Tom Keune), who are brought to trial. One of the movie's prongs follows American Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson (Michael Shannon), who fights hard for a war crimes trial for which there is no legal precedent. The larger, second prong is the interaction between American psychiatrist Douglas Kelley (Rami Malek) and Hermann Göring, which eventually includes Göring's wife, Emmy (Lotte Verbeek), and daughter, Edda (Fleur Bremmer). Translator Howie Triest (Leo Woodall) is also significant."Nuremberg" attempts to do too much, devoting time to Jackson's quest, but tells an incomplete and American-centric story. This is overwhelmed by the more interesting, and closer to the film's message, interaction and near friendship between Kelley and Göring, as Kelley discerns Göring's brilliance and recognizes the danger posed by narcissistic charismatic political leaders. Women have little role in this film, mostly there for "support" and decoration. Even Emmy could have been developed further.If you're unhappy with the state of politics in America, you may like this "Nuremberg" and wonder why that country has never joined the International Court of Justice, which is modelled on the Nuremberg trials.

Nuremberg is an entertaining treatment of the trial of top Nazi Hermann Goering. Its aim is to be crowd pleasing but also to touch on serious matters, and it succeeds. Russell Crowe is getting all the attention but Rami Malek worked better for me. John Slattery is commanding. Leo Woodall is attention-getting in a smaller role. He has a scene toward the end of the film that made me cry. There are some inaccuracies. Nuremberg addresses the Nazi persecution of Jews to the exclusion of other victims, including handicapped people, Poles, Soviet POWs, gay people, JWs, and others. But that's a minor complaint about a good movie that manages to both entertain and treat difficult material.

Paper thin. After all this time, and in this political climate, this movie had nothing original to say about the Holocaust or the Nuremberg trials. The movie had no depth, and the drama was false or undeserving.The dialogue was highly expository and awkwardly had characters talk about basic facts of WWII and about themselves that they would never actually have verbalized because it should have gone without saying, but the writers felt it necessary to pander to an undereducated audience. Why would a character have to continually remind another character who they are?The movie was incredibly tonally inconsistent, with characters cracking jokes and then suddenly being despondent. The score would swell for a scene as if there was some kind of dramatic buildup, even though the characters weren't moving the plot forward at all. In multiple scenes, scary music plays while Göring is just doing pushups, as if he's somehow an evil genius preparing to free himself and needs to be in peak condition.Russell Crowe's performance is totally wasted - his evil does not shine through at all, and the scary music is totally unearned by the script and editing and pacing.The movie has absolutely zero buildup. The plot meanders around for an hour and then suddenly they're at the trial and the music blares like we were waiting for the trial the whole time. The movie can't pick a lane between a Holocaust movie and a courtroom drama. And then it just peters out after the first day of the trial as if they somehow already won.Victorious music swells after the first trial day, after Michael Shannon's character fails at questioning Göring and the British prosecutor stands up to take his place and continues his basic questioning for him. Then they both throw meaningful looks at Kelley like he somehow was responsible for them being able to defeat Göring in this scene, even though the evidence they used to counter Göring's testimony has nothing to do with Kelley's psychological profiling and was merely historical fact they recited. Like the psychologist's insight somehow helped them destroy Göring's character, even though when the British prosecutor took over for Michael Shannon to question Göring, he didn't use any of Rami Malek's character's findings whatsoever.The movie was full of cheesy, cliché scenes - like Michael Shannon and Rami Malek meeting in the rain in trench coats to speak for two minutes about things that would've just taken place in an office, just so they can make a hamfisted reference to a stadium where Hitler gave a speech.There was extremely poor chemistry between almost all characters, with far too big a cast to devote the amount of time and dialogue needed to develop an emotional connection to the characters. For example, there's an attempted romance between Kelley and a reporter that goes nowhere and has no emotional depth. Douglas Kelley becomes a surrogate father figure to Göring's family out of nowhere. Rami Malek's emotional range in this movie consisted of him staring blankly into space for minutes on end. It didn't feel like the characters actually knew each other for thousands of hours, but like they met on set. Nowhere near enough dialogue was dedicated to feeling an attachment to or betrayal from Göring.Incredibly sappy scenes where the translator character is crying and Rami Malek is again staring off-screen for like two minutes while the translator Howie (Woodall) is just repeatedly licking and biting his lips because he doesn't have another way to display that he's holding back tears. Not to mention, when he was giving his backstory, no one from Holland back then would have called it Holland - obvious Americanization.The movie forgets about all the other Nazi characters immediately after introducing them and then randomly brings one of them back near the end.At one point near the end, Rami Malek's character turns over a King on a deck of cards in an absolutely hamfisted, amateur, bromidic metaphor for Göring. 
Watch famous moments from the real trial instead.

Bugonia might be one of Yorgos' tamer films in recent times, but it's still quintessentially him.Bugonia is one wild ride, and it works for two main reasons. The first is the incredible and convincing performances from Emma Stone andJesse Plemons (not to take away from Delbis). They bring the already sharp script to life, carrying every scene with intensity. The patient, quiet dialogue exchanges that build into sweeping orchestral crescendos really drive the bigger moments home.The second reason Bugonia works so well is the subtle, almost subconscious doubts it plants in the viewer's mind. The film challenges our own perceptions of what's real, a clever way to keep the story engaging and prevent it from ever feeling sluggish.Ultimately, though, it's the ending that defines the movie. It's a bold choice that will split audiences, some might find it ridiculous while others will applaud its courage. Personally, I think without that ending, Bugonia would've fallen into the realm of the generice thriller we've all seen before. Instead, it's audacious and unrestrained.Bugonia had the nerve to be different, to challenge its audience and storytelling conventions. It's Yorgos at his best, and without a doubt, one of my favourites of the year.

Don't get me wrong, Emma Stone is terrific here, carrying that same cool, unreadable spark that Tilda Swinton built a career on, only with a younger, brighter edge. Stone has already collected two Oscars, though, and what really catches you off guard is Jesse Plemons, who turns in a performance so sharp and so unsettling that you keep thinking you've never quite seen him push himself like this."Bugonia" eases in with what looks like a simple setup, just two men talking, one dominating the dialogue while the other tries to keep pace, and before you realize it the whole thing has shifted into a story that moves fast yet stays grounded enough to feel like something that could unfold a few blocks from where you live. I was hooked from the first scene and stayed that way nearly all the way through, though the ending lingers longer than it needs to, just enough to place it a step below "Poor Things." Even so, it is unmistakably a Yorgos Lanthimos production, and it carries that same strange, irresistible flavor that makes his work so easy to sink into.

How do I even start this? I think I need a second viewing. That sounds about right. This is such a good film, one of those where you completely lose track of time in the best way possible.The story follows Teddy, a deeply disturbed man who's convinced that aliens have infiltrated Earth to control or destroy humanity. That belief becomes the core of the film: a critique of society's structure.Then there's Michelle, a CEO type with every stereotype you can imagine: the 4:30 a.m. Wake-ups, the cold discipline, the deep disregard for the people under her. It's comically illustrated when she says her workers should leave at 17:30 but then makes it blurry signaling this is something she doesn't actually expect.Teddy has this analogy about bees, how they work tirelessly for a queen who doesn't care about any of them individually. It's a simple idea, but the way the film uses it says a lot about hierarchy, power, and blind obedience.Misinformation and the Loops We Live InWe live surrounded by misinformation, but more than that, by these endless cycles that trap us inside our own ideas. Algorithms feed us what we already believe, keeping us engaged but also more entrenched. Teddy is the perfect example of that, we see him at work listening to conspiracy podcasts he calls "research." It's all self-reinforcing, and it's frighteningly real.Trauma as FoundationAnother major theme here is trauma. From the start, we're left asking: why? Why does Teddy see the world this way? Why Michelle, specifically?It slowly becomes clear that Teddy lives almost entirely isolated from others, his only real connection being Don, someone he mostly controls. His mother becomes the central figure in understanding his paranoia. She suffered irreversible damage from a medical trial run by Michelle's company, and that event planted the seeds of distrust in him from a young age.There's a stunning black-and-white memory sequence that stood out to me, Michelle visits Teddy's family to "apologize." We see Teddy as he is now, but he's clutching to his mother on an hospital bed like a balloon, signaling that he was a child during this memory. It's a subtle, haunting way of showing how that trauma froze him in time. Later, with Casey the cop (played in a great cameo by Starvos), we start to understand that Teddy's trauma goes even deeper probably involving some kind of sexual abuse. It's heavy, but it gives context to his warped worldview.Manipulation and PowerManipulation runs through everything in Bugonia. Even in what we call "normal" society, manipulation is a fundamental part of how we function, it's how people achieve their needs or maintain control.We see this clearly with Michelle's corporate behavior, but also with Teddy's control over Don. Don clearly doesn't want to go as far as they do (the chemical castration scene says it all) but Teddy pushes him with emotional manipulation. It's darkly ironic that Teddy, who rails against power structures, ends up mimicking them himself. He becomes, unknowingly, the very "queen" he claims to hate.Michelle never really manages to manipulate Teddy into believing she's an alien. The shift happens almost by accident when the electrocution test doesn't kill her, which Teddy interprets as proof she's a "royal." That one twist of luck seals both their fates.The SpiralThe first two acts are fantastic, tense, darkly funny, layered but the third act takes things to another level.Don's death hits hard. You feel his growing awareness that they've gone too far, that none of this was ever real. Teddy, realizing both Casey and Don are dead, descends into a frantic, unstable state. Michelle seizes the moment, manipulating him into killing his own mother so she can escape. But in a brilliant touch, Michelle's escape fails because she's too injured to climb the stairs and notices what appears to be a door.Behind it: the true horror. She isn't the first. Teddy's done this before. The walls are lined with past victims, and that revelation shatters her remaining grip on reality.When Teddy returns, both of them are in full panic, not just physical chaos but psychological collapse. I loved how Yorgos shows this through movement: Michelle, once too injured to climb stairs, suddenly sprints up them. It's a visual cue that she's beginning to detach from reality.When the story returns to the company, everything falls into place. Michelle's plan is clear. She'll entrap Teddy and escape. The "teleportation" scene is so unexpected it just left me baffled.The Ending and What It MeansAfter Michelle is struck in the head, she wakes up in an ambulance, panicked, and rushes back to the office. She's clutching the calculator, trying to reach the "mothership" before the moon cycle ends and somehow, it works.But this isn't sci-fi logic, it's psychological breakdown. She's in shock, her mind splintered by trauma. The ship we see mirrors Teddy's own drawings. When she decides to "erase" humanity, bursting the atmosphere (with the darkly funny reveal that the planet is flat) it's not literal, it's symbolic. Animals survive, suggesting that she's rejecting humanity itself, not life.To me, it's not about whether Michelle is an alien. She's not. Her final act feels like a collapse of empathy and meaning, a commentary on how deeply broken the structures we live in really are.The Bigger PictureThis movie's critique feels painfully real when you think of corporations like Amazon, boasting $9.5 billion in pre-tax profits while firing unionized drivers and running aggressive union-busting campaigns. Remember the news drivers were forced to urinate in bottles to meet impossible quotas?That's Bugonia's point: we don't have to live like this. The system is built on exploitation dressed up as efficiency, and it runs on manipulation disguised as ambition.Final ThoughtsIt's clear by now that I absolutely loved this film. Emma Stone and Jesse Plemons are extraordinary, they channel both intensity and fragility so well. The sound design, cinematography, and direction are impeccable.Thank you, Yorgos, for another art piece.

And all in all an exciting and entertaining movie with surprising twists. How many times can you leave the theatre feeling refreshed and inspired, because you know you have just watched something you have never seen on a screen before? Watching *Bugonia* felt strange in the best possible way. Lanthimos throws you into a world where nothing feels entirely normal - the rules are odd, people react in unpredictable ways, and yet something about all this chaos feels oddly familiar. You laugh, but there's always tension underneath it, like you're waiting for something to go wrong. The emotions hit harder than expected, even in moments that seem absurd on paper.The story follows two conspiracy-obsessed men who kidnap Michele (played by Emma Stone), a corporate figure they believe is an alien trying to destroy Earth. It sounds ridiculous - and it is - but Lanthimos uses that absurdity to dig into paranoia, power, and the strange ways people cling to belief when faced with uncertainty.Visually, the film looks beautiful and a bit unsettling. Shooting on 35mm gives it texture - the kind of imperfections, shadows, and lighting you don't get with digital. It makes the world feel alive, slightly out of sync, and that's exactly what this story needs. The camera work feels intentional without being flashy, every frame adding to the unease.The tone is darkly funny but emotionally sharp. Lanthimos doesn't offer easy answers or explanations. He just builds tension through behavior - through silence, through glances, through moments that should be funny but end up being uncomfortable. Emma Stone stands out; she plays Michele with a mix of calm control and quiet menace that holds the film together.It's one of those films that doesn't fully explain itself, and maybe that's the point. You either go along with its strange rhythm or you don't. For me, it worked - not because everything made sense, but because it felt honest in its chaos. Lanthimos doesn't tell you what to think, he just lets the madness unfold, and somehow, that's what makes it stick.**Verdict:** 9/10 - not as tight as *The Favourite*, but easily Lanthimos's boldest and most unpredictable work since *The Lobster*..

Director Yorgos Lanthimos brings us back exactly to where he left us with Kinds of Kindness: American suburbs, conspiracy theories. Bugonia feels like the fourth episode of his anthology. Who knows, it might even be.Bugonia is a remake of the Korean movie Saving the Green Planet.It tells the story of two cousins, Teddy and Donny, who live by themselves. Teddy, the sharper one, feeds himself and his cousin with conspiracy theories, while Donny (portrayed with clear neurodivergent traits) follows him with devotion.They kidnap CEO Emma Stone, accusing her of being an Andromeda alien, and demand that she contact her colleagues so they can leave Earth and let it be at peace again - bringing back, among other things, the well-being of bees.We quickly realize that Teddy has been personally affected by Emma Stone's company: his mother is still in an induced coma because of the drugs she took from them. It becomes clear that Teddy's delusions are also driven by these personal implications.Teddy (and Donny, secondarily) is the typical example of the isolated internet addict: spending excessive time online and turning into an irrational, disconnected being. In contrast, Emma Stone is shown at the beginning of the movie creating promotional material for her company, where the script includes the word "diversity" more than X times. The movie wants to show us the two sides of today's America, and how their clash can only result in extreme and dangerous encounters.The theme is nothing new and perhaps lacks a more impactful message. There is, however, an interesting analogy between bees (alien-like creatures operating efficiently and without distracting human feelings) and humans, who - when seen from an alien perspective - seem to make the most irrational decisions: killing each other through wars, destroying our own habitat, or wasting time and attention on futilities (a theme also reflected in the final scene). But the underlying message doesn't seem to be the movie's main concern; its real value lies in the execution.Bugonia does a terrific job of entertaining the audience. It knows when to be funny and when to build tension. The dramatic music choices are particularly effective and give pace to the movie. The audience is on edge the whole way, constantly asking: "What if she really is an alien?" The movie plays with this doubt and even makes fun of us for believing it could be true - subtly reminding us we may not be in the best position to mock conspiracy theories.The movie falls short in its final minutes, when it is clumsily revealed that the CEO was, in fact, an alien. While this seems intended to be either surprising or funny, it lands as neither. By then, the audience has already entertained the possibility several times and dismissed it, because it would make little sense logically or dramatically. Nevertheless, it seems Yorgos Lanthimos either decided to follow the original story beyond what best served this film (by keeping that final scene), or he simply chose to "prank" the audience with an unsatisfying finale. But if the prank isn't funny, is it really worth it?

22 years later, Yorgos Lanthimos dares to remake the 2003 Korean masterpiece "Save the Green Planet!" by Jang Joon-hwan.Despite my love for Lanthimos, this film, unfortunately, doesn't quite deliver the same gut-wrenching agony as the original-even though the execution is technically stunning. I'm genuinely torn about how to feel about it.Let's start by saying: it's not a bad film, but it's not a great one either. This time, I'll take a slightly different approach-comparing both films to see where each shines and falters, while keeping things spoiler-free.The first thing you'll notice-if you've seen both versions-is the colour palette. "Save the Green Planet!" embraces dark greens and blues, while "Bugonia" opts for rich oranges and reds.Both are effective in building a sense of threat, but-and that's my opinion-the green hues serve the story better. The orange, however, feels perfectly aligned with Lanthimos's current aesthetic.Keeping the same tones as the original would have felt like pure imitation, so going for a warmer colors make it feel more contemporary and ominous.Both films run around two hours, yet "Bugonia" lost me halfway through-and by "lost", I mean I nearly dozed off. It's weighed down by dialogue that easily slips into rhetoric and monotony, whereas "Save the Green Planet!" balances its dialogue with bursts of violent action."Save the Green Planet!" dances along the edge of psychological horror and physical discomfort, even flirting with torture territory. "Bugonia"has its moments of violence and splatter, but never reaches the same level of unsettling intensity.A remake shouldn't be a carbon copy of its source, and in that sense, Lanthimos leaves his unmistakable Hollywood fingerprint. Still, Joon-hwan's film feels far more decayed and dystopian-a film of a time, the 2000s-when politically correct wasn't yet an invisible law.However, "Bugonia" is more polished, more accessible, clearly tailored for a broader audience. That accessibility also reshapes its perspective-and that's where the two directors diverge most.The direction, of course, differs greatly-two directors, two cultural lenses. Joon-hwan thrives in the grit and chaos of the working class, while Lanthimos prefers the stylised decay of wealth.Both handle the class divide with flair, but through entirely different textures.Performance-wise, both casts are solid. Emma Stone's portrayal of Michelle arguably fits better for the role; her shaved head and eerie makeup sharpen her ambiguity.Conversely, Baek Yoon-shik's Kang Man-shik lacks her magnetism but compensates with raw, unsettling force-his maleness also allows Joon-hwan to push certain boundaries further.It's not a gender issue, but a difference in how far each director dares to go within their respective cinematic climates.Interestingly, the gender swap extends beyond the lead conspirator. In "Save the Green Planet!," the abettor is a girl, Su-ni (Hwang Jung-min), whereas in "Bugonia" it's a boy, Don (Aidan Delbis).This shift subtly changes the emotional dynamics, even though some of the empathy between captor and captive remains intact.As for the mastermind behind the abduction: Teddy, played by Jesse Plemons-an actor I'd protect at all costs-feels a bit muted here. In contrast, Shin Ha-kyun's Lee Byeong-gu in the original radiates psychotic energy and conviction.The endings have sparked endless online debates, and truthfully, both work within their respective worlds. They hit different emotional notes but leave the same pit in your stomach.Both films hold a mirror to our species-fractured, hopeful, and cruel, highlighting the same uncomfortable question about humanity that feels increasingly urgent today. Watch both, then decide for yourself.As for me? My allegiance remains clear-I'm still all in to "Save the Green Planet!" Sorry, Lanthimos, but this time you didn't quite abduct me.

Yorgos Lanthimos is back doing his usual weird thing with Bugonia. Both are harrowing and spectacular (this is Plemons best part ever) but are also limited by the linearity of it all. Bugonia: "Ox Birth" A fictional method where bees are spontaneously generated from an Ox's carcass.Bugonia is a movie focusing of human alienation, in terms of privilege on both ends of the extreme and human self-destruction. The story centers on Teddy Gatz (Jesse Plemons), a beekeeper and alien conspiracy theorist who has decided he must save the world. Teddy, who lives in an isolated family home with his simple and reluctant cousin/accomplice, Don, has become alienated, living solely in a world of online quackery. Teddy believes an overarching conspiracy by the alien race, the Andromedins, is the true cause of suffering, rather than corporate greed.They kidnap Michelle Fuller (Emma Stone), the head of a PR-savvy biomedical conglomerate. Michelle is characterized by her use of corporate jargon and a veneer of accountability to cover business interests. Teddy's plan is to use Michelle as a hostage/ambassador to contact the Andromedins and negotiate a settlement for them to leave Earth alone from their secret control. The conflict however has a personal root, Michelle was heading the failed clinical trial that resulted in Teddy's mother's coma, questioning if his intention is "human salvation" or self-serving revenge.Michelle constantly balances between horribly alien and weirdly human. Shaving her hair and covering her in cream make her appear an otherworldly creature, yet her singing, crying, and screaming are all too human. She admits to Teddy that she sees she has become a person she swore she would never be through her corporate cover ups, recognizing her own alien elements in seeking corporate over human interests.The dialogue between them is sharp, hilarious and thought provoking. Michelle's attempts to psychologically control Teddy are shattered when he reveals his (and Don's) chemical castration to limit their attraction, shocking her into understanding their fanaticism. Michelle is then forced to conform to his delusion, spinning tales of Atlantis and a Yacoubian genetic plot to fit her role as an alien royal.The turning point occurs when Don self-exits. Don functions as an audience stand in and the moderating presence, whose humanity and disgust with the torture constantly strain his love for Teddy. Without Don, the conflict becomes to the death. The violence escalates with the killing of a cop, maiming, the killing of Teddy's comatose mother with antifreeze, and the final infiltration of Michelle's workplace with Don's body in the back. The humanity Teddy sought to portray is cast aside, and Michelle's survival depends on leaning further into her alienating qualities.The movie is fantastic up through the ambulance scene, but the ending creates a massive tonal shift. The film resolves the ambiguity, confirming that Teddy was right (Michelle was a real alien). In an Orphean tragedy, He also leads humanity to its doom as he represents human fatalism at its worst through his violence and serial murder to the mostly benevolent Andromedins. Michelle returns to the mothership and, after lamenting about being corrupted, convinces them to end the human experiment. Everyone dies as humanity is deemed self-destructive and irredeemable.Had the film retained the element of ambiguity (leaving Michelle in uncertainty) on what dilutes our humanity and makes us alien, it would have been much stronger. Yet ultimately it is a gorgeous and deviously funny film well worth the runtime.

Yorgos Lanthimos and Emma Stone's Overdone PartnershipYorgos Lanthimos and Emma Stone have undeniably created some striking films together, from The Favourite to Poor Things. Their collaborations often blend sharp surrealism with Stone's fearless performances, delivering moments of brilliance that linger. But let's be honest: their relentless streak of projects is starting to feel like a one-note symphony.The issue isn't talent-Lanthimos's offbeat vision and Stone's chameleon-like acting are still top-tier. It's the sheer frequency. Back-to-back films with the same director-actor duo can sap the freshness from even the most inventive premises. Their latest efforts, while polished, echo the same quirky, detached tone and stylized weirdness that defined their earlier work. It's like watching a brilliant chef cook the same dish repeatedly-eventually, you crave a new flavor.Stone's commitment to Lanthimos's eccentric worlds is admirable, but her constant presence risks turning their films into a predictable shtick. The audience deserves variety, and both artists are versatile enough to explore beyond this partnership. A break to work with other directors or actors could reinvigorate their craft and give us something new to savor. For now, this once-exciting collaboration feels like it's overstayed its welcome, leaving a stale aftertaste.

While watching Bugonia, I gradually stopped approaching it as a conventional sci-fi or conspiracy film and began reading it as a metaphor built from the film's own events and imagery. The characters at the bottom of the hierarchy are repeatedly shown performing, reacting, and suffering within a system they neither control nor fully understand-evoking the image of worker bees sustaining a larger structure.One moment that stood out occurs when the powerful figure played by Emma Stone authorizes financial compensation for the protagonist's mother after a product-related fault. Within the film, this action is presented as responsibility or resolution, yet it feels limited. The system responds efficiently to a material or legal failure, but later, when human lives themselves are at stake, that same sense of obligation disappears. The contrast is created by the film's own progression, not external commentary.The ending reinforces this imbalance. Emma Stone's character ultimately leaves, and the film allows the consequences for humanity to unfold without intervention. Interpreted symbolically, this resembles how, in nature, a queen bee abandons a hive when survival is no longer viable, leaving the worker bees behind. The film does not explain this choice-it simply shows it, letting the implications speak for themselves.The repeated use of the term "alien" also feels deliberate. These figures are not presented as alien solely because of extraterrestrial origin, but because of how they appear and behave: visibly altered, emotionally distant, and detached from ordinary human vulnerability. Within the film's visual language, their artificiality creates a sense that they are no longer fully human. This aligns with contemporary imagery of extreme self-modification and constructed identities, though the film never states this directly-it allows the resemblance to emerge naturally.Seen this way, Bugonia does not frame humanity's collapse as the result of an external invasion, but as the outcome of distance, hierarchy, and abandonment. The film leaves viewers to sit with the discomfort rather than offering resolution.Rather than delivering a clear message, Bugonia works as a reflective piece-one that invites the viewer to ask whether the system shown on screen values people as individuals, or only as long as they serve a function.

It's finally here, a Predator movie that doesn't take itself too seriously, yet remains incredibly well-made and thoroughly entertaining, Dan Trachtenberg, who already delivered the most serious and still the best Predator film to date with Prey, is clearly having a blast with Predator: Badlands, from the very first scene, the movie hooks you with one of the most exciting and promising intros in the franchise.This is the closest we've ever gotten to seeing the Predator as an actual character, complete with personality, language, and depth, and it works remarkably well, adding to that, Elle Fanning is a great addition to the film, and the little creature named Bud also brings unexpected charm to the film.Besides being one of the most excitingly entertaining films of the year, Predator: Badlands, in my opinion, the most wholesome buddy cop movie i've seen in a while, the beautifully shot, vast, and dark Predator world gives off Dune vibes for me, while the introduction of fascinating new creatures evokes a touch of Avatar, i genuinely adore the world building they've did in the film, it's visually stunning.The action and fight sequences are exciting, and the Predator is as badass as ever, while the pacing slows down in the second half, overall, Predator: Badlands is pure fun, exciting, and wildly entertaining, i wouldn't mind another installment, as long as Dan Trachtenberg returns to direct it, because honestly, the best Predator movies are the last three, all under his direction.

This movie was highly anticipated by me. I am a fan of not only the movie, but more importantly, the comics! Anyone who is only watching the movies, is missing the backstories and sequels to the movies. I won't make this a long winded review, you can scroll anywhere else and read those. This is more of a "why" to the direction of the movie.I'm glad I allowed myself to be open to new ideas regarding the franchise. This movie played to the comics ideas of the Predator aka the Yautja, and showed actual depth to them. It's very easy to get caught up in the idea of them being a villain only, and never understanding who they're an actual villain too and why. Like running into a tiger in the woods. It could kill you and still look majestic asf later while playing with its cub lol. The movie Predator gives us the look into the culture and family life of the Yautja. You don't see human interaction or hunting of humans. You see the evolution of a Predator and why its honor and anger are so one and the same. The lust for a better hunt is explained in the comics well and now for the first time, on screen from the side of the Predator. This is again, comic driven. Yes the comics get gory and graphic, but not all of them are about that too. This was a wonderful set up for future movies to follow. The action was on point. The comedic relief was needed. It's Disney being Disney and grooming the next wave of fans. Some of the characters are added in there I believe to make this less of a monster movie and more of an action movie. We have the horror style Predators. I feel like those did very little to expand the fan base and secure it for more generations to come. The horror style played to the already existing theme that older fans wanted to see.Go see the movie and make your own conclusions. After that, look up the comics. There's so much more story that is explained outside of the big screen.

I have conflicted feelings about this one. There's a strong sense of immaturity watching this film, the Disneyfication of Predator franchise, there's no denying that. We have the classic Disney theme of friends on an adventure, with cute xeno-species and plenty of morale-preaching and for-exposition-only dialogue you'd think a Predator would put an end to with a well aimed shot from a shoulder-mounted plasma cannon. There's even a couple of shots copying (or was it stealing?) from the Fellowship of the Ring, with the fellowship advancing along a mountain ridge path (you'll know it when you see it).Like a few others have said, if I squint my eyes just a little, this is Predator in the name only -- it could have been any other franchise on another world that makes little difference as the plot advances along the lines that feel all too familiar. Then, just as the plot takes a turn you'd think would add the much needed complexity, it was just another arch-villain. Then everything is tied neatly back into what is Disney's well tried story scheme, the closest you'll get to a "happily ever after".I'll be frank -- there's plenty of people who would love this movie, especially in current period I consider a drought in cinema. Badlands isn't as bad as some of the other movies of this franchise, it's just that it resolutely and confidently leaps along the same direction that its predecessors had to crawl along. So in essence, it's just a better made bad Predator movie IMO.The bad part is that it has stripped the franchise of what in my mind constituted the value here -- a cunning, intelligent predator of _different_ intelligence and ethics/morale, that comes head to head with the homo sapiens, another prominent killer made by evolution, with gore worthy of David Cronenberg. Predator franchise has never been Cannes material exactly, but it also never was Disney-like resignation to cookie-cutter villainry. Now it has the distinction of only avoiding the former.Perhaps the cinematic medium is dead for this kind of film. Interestingly enough, I am quite hyped for Killer of Killers by the same director. It seems animation attracts fewer vultures, giving the people who understand what they want, more freedom to get that done. This has Disney product sales department written all over it. Or let's call it Teen Predator: Badlands.Giving it a 6 because of the action scenes and the fact the plot isn't one short straight line at least.

Predator: Badlands is what happens when a studio strays so far from the sci-fi horror roots of the franchise that you can barely recognise the world you once loved. The tension, the grit, the primal fear that made the originals unforgettable, none of it survives here. Instead, we get glossy CGI fireworks, hollow lore dumps, and characters who wander through the story like they're immune to common sense. The Predator, once a terrifying apex hunter, now feels about as threatening as a malfunctioning parade float. Disney's influence hangs over the whole thing: every bold idea sanded down, every bit of personality replaced with something safe, sanitised, and painfully market-tested. As someone who grew up with these films, watching this felt strangely heartbreaking like coming home expecting something familiar and comforting, only to find it replaced with Snow White wearing a Predator mask. It left me with a genuine ache, almost like homesickness for a franchise that used to respect its own identity. And honestly, when will Disney learn that stripping away what made the original work special doesn't help anybody fans, newcomers, or the story itself?

The recent films have completely lost the suffocating horror and nerve-wracking tension that defined the first two entries. It feels like the writers no longer understand the true essence of the Yautja. In the original film, it wasn't just a mindless killer - it was a calculating hunter. Remember how it used its toxic dart to paralyze its prey before firing the plasma caster? Its weapon wasn't just for destruction; it could adjust its power and precision. That level of detail made the Yautja terrifying - a cold, silent, methodical predator who hunted one victim at a time, unseen, and only revealed itself when absolutely necessary or when its cloaking device was damaged.Sadly, that cold-blooded patience and ritualistic style of hunting are gone in the newer installments. The creature feels more like a generic monster than the disciplined hunter that once embodied fear and intelligence. I truly hope Jim and John Thomas return to write, and that John McTiernan steps back into the director's chair. Only they can restore the primal fear, intensity, and cinematic tension that made Predator legendary.

Predator: Badlands opens a rare window into the inner world and culture of the Yautja. It succeeds at nearly everything it attempts: introducing fresh monsters, exploring Weyland-Yutani robotics, and expanding the universe in interesting ways.That said, the film leans a bit too heavily into emotional themes such as trauma, family bonds, and even the feelings of synthetic beings. While these elements add depth, they sometimes feel redundant.Still, the movie is undeniably fun. The EvidencePositivesThe opening minutes suggest purpose. The framing, contrast, and scale imply a film that might take its time and trust its images.There is an early sense of texture and grounded science fiction that could have developed into something intellectually stimulating.The central concept, a young hunter on a rite-of-passage trial, holds potential to explore Predator culture through a fresh point of view.Visually, the production is competent. The cinematography is stable, the lighting well balanced, and the visual effects merge smoothly with practical design.The sound design does its job with clarity, establishing atmosphere even when tension falters.There is one engaging visual moment, a full tracking shot that follows a descent sequence from start to finish, showing what this film could have been if it had committed to visual authorship.NegativesCreative choices are overly safe. The film follows a predictable action formula and rarely finds its own rhythm or visual identity.The script overexplains. Instead of cinematic discovery, the story tells the audience what to think, removing the tension of uncertainty.Communication between leads is handled with excessive convenience. A language barrier that could deepen immersion is replaced with quick translation, stripping away mystery.The movie avoids silence. Dialogue or exposition fills nearly every moment, leaving little space for suspense or curiosity.Slow motion feels decorative rather than poetic. In films where it works, slow motion reveals perception or emotion that cannot be seen in real time. Think "Superman noticing The Flash" or "The Flash catching Bruce Wayne's batarang." Here, slow motion reads as "this looks cool" rather than "this reveals truth," undermining the visceral speed hunting scenes require.The PG-13 tone is obvious. The grit and fear that once defined the series are replaced by a commercial, family-safe presentation.Creature design is strategically softened. The younger Yautja's more human, marketable features read like an aesthetic compromise rather than an organic reflection of lore.Culture and hierarchy feel human rather than alien. Familiar family drama dynamics are applied where unique logic and custom should lead.The gender and competence distribution feels engineered rather than organic, frequently reassigning capability away from the lead.The protagonist's journey lacks agency. He is guided, corrected, and rescued so often that growth rarely feels earned.The companion dynamic undermines tension. Constant guidance functions like an in-story walkthrough, removing survival stakes.Worldbuilding flirts with imagination but never defines its own physics or logic. Few environmental rules distinguish this place from Earth.The visual tone is polished but anonymous. No singular image or frame asserts authorship.Pacing is mechanical. Scenes move through checkpoints rather than breathing into themes or relationships.The climax resolves with convenience more than consequence. The arc closes without convincingly internalized growth.Character pairing reads engineered to broaden rating and reach. It feels like a workaround to avoid an R rating rather than a story-driven choice.At times it plays like humans cosplaying as Predators inside franchise fan fiction. Alien strangeness is softened toward human behavior, and the synthetic presence behaves like a human stand-in.Technology logic gap. The film presents Yautja spacecraft and weaponry far beyond human capability, yet the most competent on-screen tech belongs to a human-built android. There is no depiction of Yautja scientific culture, makers, labs, or doctrine to justify those advances, and no scouting intelligence that explains why a hunter arrives uninformed about a lethally documented world.Primitive combat philosophy. Despite millennia of hunting and superior tools, close-quarters fighting reads like basic human brawling. There is no distinct martial grammar or tactics that express an alien philosophy of movement.Absent sensory signature. Earlier entries branded the senses with thermal vision, oppressive soundscapes, environmental heat and humidity, and tactile menace. Here, those cues barely register, so the film rarely makes you feel the hunt.The score is competent but indistinct. It offers no motif, identity, or thematic evolution. Strong franchises often use music to bridge eras. Stallone's 2008 "Rambo" reintroduces the classic theme at an emotional peak to ground identity, and "Casino Royale" withholds the Bond theme until the identity is earned. "Badlands" offers no such bridge and no echo of Alan Silvestri's Predator motif to bind past to present.The TestimonyPredator: Badlands opens like a film with direction. Its first impressions suggest ambition, a return to cinematic patience and scale. The longer it runs, the more it trades risk for comfort. Where there should be discovery, there is instruction. Where there could be mystery, there is translation. The camera explains instead of revealing.The lead Yautja's softened, human-like proportions suggest a boardroom adjustment for wider appeal. If the intention is to portray a younger hunter, the film does not contextualize the difference. The change reads cosmetic rather than cultural.The rating calculus is visible. Choices around pairing and communication feel less like bold storytelling and more like a mechanism to widen the audience. The production often resembles franchise fan fiction: humans cosplaying as Predators, a synthetic presence behaving like a human proxy, and the strangeness that should define this world is smoothed away.Culturally, isolation hurts most. Beginning on the Predator homeworld should open a door to daily life and intellectual infrastructure. We never glimpse who designs ships, who iterates weapons, or how knowledge is taught and transmitted. There are no labs, makers, scholars, scout corps, or doctrinal rules of engagement. The story asks us to accept hyper-advanced hardware while depicting a hunter who arrives ignorant of dangers his society already chronicles. If prior expeditions died there, someone survived to report, or a probe returned. The absence of that logic weakens the premise.On the ground, fighting expresses the same contradiction. A species that refines tools across ages would also refine movement. Yet close-quarters exchanges read like plain human brawls, not an alien martial philosophy. When technology signals excellence but tactics signal guesswork, the world feels assembled rather than lived in.The sensory language is where a Predator story should sing. Thermal vision should reframe the battlefield. The mix should creep and suffocate. Air should feel wet or thin. Heat should distort. Surfaces should scrape. Instead, sensory memory is faint. The film seldom imprints the hunt on your nerves.Even in music, the film misses an identity bridge. "Rambo" and "Casino Royale" show how legacy motifs can be used sparingly but decisively to connect eras. Badlands never grants that sonic dividend.In the end, the film could have been the missing chapter that reveals how these hunters evolve into the being we met in the jungle with Schwarzenegger, or a narrative prelude that connects to that lineage. A clever callback or final reveal might have bridged this origin to the legend. Instead, it closes as an isolated concept rather than a living chapter of a saga.

If there's ever been a film that carries the name "Predator" yet completely fails to grasp even the most basic essence of the franchise - its rhythm, atmosphere, or sense of threat - that film is undoubtedly Predator: Badlands. At best, it can be described as a failed exercise in mimicking a legend - a film devoid of the Predator's spirit, menace, and that primal suspense that defined the originals.The director clearly has no understanding of the Predator universe. In an attempt to recreate tension and violence through cheap digital effects and noisy framing, he has only produced visual chaos. Scenes that should feel grand or mysterious are instead filled with illogical lighting, aimless editing, and an overall lack of visual reasoning. The whole thing feels more like a pretentious student project, where the filmmaker has confused "personal style" with "visual disorder."
In Badlands, there is no character development, no narrative arc, not even a reason to care about what's happening. The characters are so shallow and faceless that by the film's midpoint, the audience has stopped caring whether they live or die. The dialogue is artificial, lifeless, and often laughable - as if written by an AI that has never actually seen an action movie.The Predator itself - the symbol of the ultimate hunter - looks more like a person in a plastic Halloween costume. The production design and visual effects are so weak that it constantly feels like a cheap '90s TV movie. Instead of inspiring fear, the film turns the Predator into a visual joke - a creature that no longer frightens, but amuses.The performances are directionless; there's no sense of control or dramatic understanding. Every move and reaction feels clichéd and hollow, and in moments meant to evoke fear or tension, the only thing that comes across is confusion.Predator: Badlands isn't just a bad movie - it's an outright assault on the cinematic legacy of the franchise. The director has proven he neither respects the mythos of Predator nor possesses the ability to create something new within it. He has reduced the Predator brand to the level of a dull YouTube video, squandering both audience trust and studio credibility.If there's any respect left for the name Predator, the first step should be removing this director from any future projects - permanently.
